paras: The attempted lynching of the Laprade murder suspects at Springfield, Tennessee, took place on the night of February 14, 1881, when a mob of about twenty-five mounted men forced a door of the town jail intending to lynch Black prisoners brought there that day for trial. The mob dispersed after Judge Joe Stark and Attorney General B. D. Bell promised an immediate trial without a change of venue, and militia from Nashville arrived at midnight. The reprieve lasted four days: on February 18 a mob of about two hundred men took five of the prisoners from the sheriff and hanged them from the court house.

The prisoners were accused of robbing and killing a farmer named Laprade near Sadlersville on September 8, 1880. An old man named Jim Higgins was said to have confessed after his feet were burned, and on September 15 two other accused men, Bell and Jamison, were lynched. Higgins's confession named James Elder, Loch Mallory, Lou and Robert Thweat, Andrew Duffy and Bill Murphy, who were held in the Nashville jail until February 14, when they were returned to Springfield for trial.

That evening Judge Stark telegraphed Governor Hawkins for twenty-five to fifty men, warning that the prisoners "were to be mobbed to-night". The governor sent fifty men of the Porter Rifles and Rock City Guards and ordered the Robertson County sheriff to summon the county.

At 10:40 p.m. about twenty-five men on horseback rode in and were joined by men who had been "lounging about the town all day". The crowd, which one later account said was armed with guns and pistols, gathered at the jail and forced one door before Stark and Bell came out to meet it.

According to the Chicago Tribune, the mob gave the judge "respectful attention" and agreed to disperse if the prisoners were tried immediately without a change of venue. Fifty militiamen under Capt. George Royer arrived by special train at midnight. Inside the jail Bill Murphy, told that the mob was coming to lynch him, tried to kill himself by butting his head against a stone wall.

On February 16 Stark discharged the militia, but the attorney general then wired the governor that without a strong guard "the prisoners will be mobbed", and the governor ordered the sheriff to summon the entire power of the county. No arrest of anyone in the February 14 mob appears in the coverage.

The trial went ahead as promised, and Murphy and Duffy, who testified for the State, were released. On the evening of February 18, after the judge's charge to the jury, about two hundred men took five prisoners from the sheriff at the court-room door and hanged them from the court-house veranda. Murphy and Duffy were reported found hanging near the scene of the murder, though the Clarksville Chronicle said they had escaped. On February 19 a resolution condemning the mob was adopted unanimously at Nashville.

The first account came from the Nashville American's Springfield correspondent and ran on February 15 and 16 in papers in Washington, Memphis, Indianapolis, Dallas, Savannah, Lancaster and Richmond. Headlines included "A Lynching Prevented" in the Evening Star, "Almost a Lynching" in the Indiana State Sentinel and "Attempt to Lynch Negro Murderers" in Dallas. The wire treated guilt as settled before trial, calling the prisoners "five negro murderers" and warning the mob might return "to carry out their programme of lynching the wretches".

The Memphis Appeal headed the story "The Laprade Murderers In Danger from the Excited Citizens of Springfield" and prefaced it with the killing as "one of the most diabolical crimes on record". After the lynching four days later, the attempt reappeared as prelude in accounts reporting that "Public sentiment sustains the action of the mob", and the American's correspondent wrote that "an outraged community could wait no longer".

Most reports gave the mob as about twenty-five horsemen, but a Memphis Appeal special said forty came and were persuaded by citizens to let the law take its course. The Memphis Appeal and a later wire account said Higgins had died in the Nashville jail after an amputation, while the Juniata Sentinel and the Clarksville correspondent named him among the five hanged.

bases: A mob forced a door of the Springfield jail intending to lynch prisoners awaiting trial and left without killing anyone, an attempted lynching (A1, A3, A12).

The Nashville American special (A1, A2), separate Chicago Tribune specials (A3) and later retrospective accounts (A12, A14) agree on the mounted mob, the forced jail door and its dispersal on the judge's promise.

accounts.gist: A mob of 25 mounted men, joined by loungers, forced a jail door and dispersed when Judge Stark and Attorney General Bell promised an immediate trial without change of venue; militia arrived at midnight.

accounts.label: Retrospective accounts after the Feb. 18 lynching
accounts.gist: Twenty-five armed mounted men came to the jail bent on taking the prisoners and left when assured of a trial and, if guilty, hanging; troops were then placed at the Court House.

framing.detail: Papers from Washington to Dallas ran the American special under 'A Lynching Prevented', 'Almost a Lynching', 'Attempt to Lynch Negro Murderers' and 'Trouble in Tennessee', calling the untried prisoners 'the wretches'.
The Memphis Appeal headed it 'The Laprade Murderers In Danger from the Excited Citizens of Springfield' and set the mob beside a graphic account of 'one of the most diabolical crimes on record'.
The Knoxville Chronicle framed the follow-up around the governor: 'Governor Hawkins is Determined to Prevent Violence'.
After the later lynching the Clarksville Chronicle's Springfield correspondent wrote that the seven 'deserved their fate' and that 'an outraged community could wait no longer'.
The long wire account reported that 'Public sentiment sustains the action of the mob' while also printing the Nashville resolution condemning it.
